nameStory: The "dolphinfish" name comes from this fish's habit of following ships and leaping out of the water like dolphins, though it's not related to marine mammals at all! It's also called "mahi-mahi" (pronounced MAH-hee-MAH-hee), which means "strong-strong" in Hawaiian, referring to its powerful swimming ability. The name "dorado" means "golden" in Spanish, highlighting its brilliant golden-yellow coloration.
description: The Common Dolphinfish is a spectacular offshore ocean fish with brilliant golden-yellow sides and a distinctive high, blunt forehead. These fast-swimming predators are built for speed, with a torpedo-shaped body and long dorsal fin that runs nearly the entire length of their back. They're medium to large fish that can reach impressive sizes, and their colors are absolutely dazzling when fresh - think living gold with electric blue and green highlights.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brilliant golden-yellow body with electric blue and green highlights that shimmer like metal in sunlight; colors fade quickly after death, so fresh fish are unmistakable

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Torpedo-shaped body built for speed, with a distinctively high, blunt forehead that feels firm and rounded to the touch

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single long dorsal fin runs almost the entire length of the back like a mohawk; tail is deeply forked and feels stiff and powerful

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Terminal mouth positioned at the front tip of the head with small, sharp teeth that feel like sandpaper when you run your finger along them

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found in open ocean waters far from shore, often near floating debris, sargassum seaweed, or following boats

habitat: In New England waters, Common Dolphinfish are found only in offshore ocean waters, typically many miles from the coast in the warm Gulf Stream currents. They're surface dwellers that prefer the open ocean, often associating with floating debris, seaweed mats, or other structures. These are warm-water fish that only appear in our northern waters during the warmest months when ocean temperatures rise.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters as ocean temperatures are still too cold for these tropical visitors.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for dolphinfish in New England waters when Gulf Stream currents bring warm water north; look for them around floating debris or sargassum patches.
seasonality.fall: Still possible to encounter in early fall during warm years, but they begin moving south as water temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having migrated south to warmer tropical and subtropical regions.

funFact: Dolphinfish are among the fastest-growing fish in the ocean - they can grow from tiny fry to 20 pounds in just one year, making them essentially the weeds of the fish world, but beautiful, delicious weeds!
confusionNotes: The name causes the most confusion - these are fish, not the intelligent marine mammals we call dolphins! Also, don't confuse them with freshwater dorado from South America, which is a completely different fish. Remember: if it's golden, has fins, and you caught it on a hook, it's the fish kind of dolphin.
contextualKnowledge: The "dolphin" name creates endless confusion since most people think of the marine mammal first. In restaurants, they're almost always called "mahi-mahi" to avoid this confusion - nobody wants to accidentally order Flipper for dinner! This naming issue is so common that many fishing guides spend time explaining that dolphinfish are completely unrelated to mammalian dolphins.
compareHints: Common Dolphinfish is the only member of its family regularly found in New England waters, making it unique in our region. The closest similar-looking fish might be large mackerel or small tunas, but none have that distinctive high, blunt forehead or the brilliant golden coloration. If you're seeing that metallic gold color in an offshore fish, you've almost certainly found a dolphinfish.
